source.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
source.authors: Ishaq Aden-Ali; Noah Golowich; Allen Liu; Abhishek Shetty; A. Moitra; Nika Haghtalab

record.tranche_reason: Tests subliminal transfer with teacher-scored selection from real preference data and DPO, rather than the original study's teacher-generated SFT data and fine-tuning setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for LLS-selected preference-data training, animal-mention and evil-persona evaluations, and empirical correlations relevant to its log-linearity account. It also reports figure-only comparisons for many animal/model combinations; individual figure values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: Tests whether a trait moves to a student through data with no overt trace of it. The trait-bearing teacher selects subsets of real tulu2.5 preference data, which train students by DPO. This replaces the original's teacher-generated SFT outputs. It measures student trait rates (animal mentions, evil-ruler responses, target language) and includes cross-family teacher/student pairs.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that Logit-Linear Selection of real preference-data subsets makes fine-tuned students behave as if system-prompted (animal preference, target language, evil persona), and that this works somewhat universally across student models, more strongly when teacher and student match. They offer log-linearity as the general explanation, with a theorem and correlation evidence. They suggest the original subliminal learning may be a special SFT case of LLS, and that number data may transfer poorly across models because its embeddings are not shared.
record.recipe_differences: Uses teacher-scored selection/reweighting of real preference data followed by DPO, rather than teacher-generated unrelated SFT outputs. Animal examples are filtered for target-animal mentions; evil-persona data are drawn from preference examples. LoRA rank 64 is reported.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer strength varies with teacher/student model match; same-model animal transfer is described as stronger than cross-model transfer. The evil-persona outcome varies by evaluation prompt and student model.
record.problems: Many behavioral values are presented only in figures, without exact numbers in the text. Animal results use a limited set of 10 evaluation prompts; the evil-persona evaluation uses GPT-5 mini as judge and 100 generations per prompt. Cross-model animal significance is stated only for many animals, not identified animal by animal.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 8–11 show additional animal/model/teacher combinations and training trajectories. Individual figure-only animal rows for those combinations were not extracted; the prose summaries for cross-model students are recorded in A11–A12. The language-transfer experiment was also omitted because it concerns a different target behavior than the listed versions.

untested.parts: Teacher-generated numbers, code or maths outputs, and SFT. Here the traits ride on teacher-scored selection of real human-written preference data trained with DPO.
Cross-base transfer with teacher-generated (number-sequence) data, the original's setting.
Emergent-misalignment benchmarks or other harmful traits beyond an evil-ruler persona judged on three prompts.
Token entanglement, divergence tokens and causal steering-vector interventions. Only the log-linear account, with update-vector correlations, is examined.
All of it. LoRA rank 64 only, no full fine-tuning, no designed variation of evaluation prompts as a robustness test.
All of it. There is no prompt-only insertion without fine-tuning.

missing.what: Olmo2-1B student mention rates in the Table 1 runs: 29.9% with OLMo teacher vs 3.2% with Qwen teacher
Animal results with Qwen3-8B and Olmo2-1B-Instruct teachers across three students. Text says a much smaller Olmo2-1B teacher still induces significant mentions for many animals
Language-transfer experiment: base ≈0 target language; Qwen3-8B and Olmo2-7B students often answer in the target language from an Olmo2-7B-selected subset. Cross-model runs fluctuate and degenerate
PCA of difference vectors: positive correlation same-model, essentially orthogonal cross-model
Evidence for approximate low logit rank and cross-model overlap of embedding subspaces, above a random baseline

record.verdict_notes: Different recipe: the trait is carried by which human-written examples are kept (top 5–10% by teacher-scored shift), not by teacher-generated text. Training is DPO with LoRA rank 64. Animal experiments filter only explicit animal mentions and have no random-subset fine-tuning control; the persona experiment does have one. Persona judging uses GPT-5 mini, three runs, peak rates over checkpoints. Appendix B.3 notes shorter response truncation gave the most striking persona transfer. The record's version codes V1–V5 were remapped to A–F, and E was removed from all rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test teacher-generated lists of numbers, code, or maths reasoning; it uses subsets of a real preference dataset.
Tests several teacher/student pairs, not all base-model combinations or a general requirement that initialization be identical.
Tests an evil-ruler persona, not other harmful traits or broader alignment outcomes.
Proposes and empirically examines log-linearity and correlated update vectors; it does not test token entanglement, divergence tokens, or a causal steering-vector mechanism.
Evaluates behavior on prompts distinct from the preference-training data. Uses LoRA rank 64 only; does not test full fine-tuning or other LoRA ranks.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning.
